# An investigation of normal-quantile plots

Exercise 3.44 in the FastR2 text seems to
suggest the shape of a normal-quantile plot
may correspond to certain shapes in the
underlying distribution.  We investigate,
first, what sort of normal-quantile plot
arises from data that is from a right-skewed
population.  I select an exponential
distribution, draw a random sample, and then
look at the corresponding normal
quantile plot.
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2
mydata = rexp(100, 1)
gf_qq(~mydata)
```

For left-skewed data, like that coming from a beta distribution
with shqpe1 = 6 and shape2 = 2, the normal quantile plot is
```{r}
#| fig-height: 2
mydatabeta = rbeta(100, shape1=6, shape2=2)
gf_qq(~mydatabeta)
```

# Simulating probabilities

### A roll-die-then-draw-token simulation

First, I want to simulate the
die-roll-token-draw probabilities.
To do it once, I might execute this code
chunk.
```{r}
bagA = c(0,0,0,0,1,1)   # 4 Red, 2 Green tokens
bagB = c(0,1,1,1,1,1)   # 1 Red, 5 Green
dieRoll = sample(c(1:3), size=1)
if (dieRoll == 1) {token=sample(bagA, size=1)} else {
  token=sample(bagB, size=1) }
token
```

We do it many times in order to learn,
via simulation, the probability of drawing
a green token:
```{r}
result = replicate(5000,
 {dieRoll = sample(c(1:3), size=1);
 if (dieRoll == 1) {token=sample(c(0,0,0,0,1,1), size=1)} else {
  token=sample(c(0,1,1,1,1,1), size=1) };
 token}
)
sum(result)/5000
```
Following these 5000 steps, I got `{r} sum(result)` greens.

### Simulating a straight flush

There must be many ways to do this. My
approach will be to think of the numbers
1--52 in groups of 13.  In alphabetical
order, perhaps the *clubs* are 1--13,
*diamonds* 14-26, *hearts* 27-39, and *spades*
40-52.  In that vein, a hand dealt to me
might be
```{r}
hand = sample(1:52, size=5)
sort(hand)
```
which translates as the

 * 4 of diamonds
 * 6 of diamonds
 * J of hearts
 * 8 of spades
 * K of spades

(Here, I am treating the aces as 1, 14, 27,
and 40.)

The main algorithm will be this:
```{r}
hand = sort(sample(c(1:52), size=5))
suits = round(hand/13)
flush = (suits[5] == suits[1])
straight = (hand[5] == hand[1] + 4)
```
If both `hand` and `flush` are TRUE, we have
a straight flush.  The exception would be the
*royal flush*, which treats an ace as the
last card in a run 10-J-Q-K-A, such as in
1-10-11-12-13, or 40-49-50-51-52.  We add
another line to check if we have one of these:
```{r}
(hand[5] == hand[2] + 3) & (hand[2] == hand[1] + 12)
```

We might define a function to which `hand`
is sent, and checks for both the flush
condition and the straight.

```{r}
straightFlush = function(hand) {
  hand = sort(hand)
  suits = round(hand/13)
  flush = (suits[5] == suits[1])
  straight = (hand[5] == hand[1] + 4) |
    ((hand[5] == hand[2] + 3) &
       (hand[2] == hand[1] + 12))
  return (flush & straight)
}

result = replicate(10000000, {
  hand = sample(c(1:52), size=5)
  straightFlush(hand)
})
sum(result)/10000000
```

The simulated probability of getting a
straight-flush is
`{r} sum(result)/10000000`.
Wikipedia says the chance of a straight-flush
is $0.00154$%.  Of course, each new run of
the code chunk above will produce a different
result.  By the **law of large numbers**,
more repetitions should bring better
approximations of the *true* probability,
but to do more than 10 million requires
even greater patience.

### Simulating a hypergeometric probability

The table on p. 99 gives rise to a data frame:
```{r}
twins <- rbind(
  do(2) * c("dizygotic", "convicted"),
  do(15) * c("dizygotic", "notConvicted"),
  do(10) * c("monozygotic", "convicted"),
  do(3) * c("monozygotic", "notConvicted")
)
colnames(twins) = c("type", "record")
head(twins)
```

We use this raw data to reconstruct the table:
```{r}
tally(type ~ record, data=twins)
```

The number convicted among monozygotic twins is 10, and
accessed from the array/table as
```{r}
tally(type ~ record, data=twins)[2,1]
```
It seems somewhat on the high side, particularly when you
view there are only 13 monozygotic twins in the study, and
the number of convicted dizygotic twins is a small
proportion of the 17 of those in the study.

But what hypotheses are we testing?  It's
$$ {\mathbf H_0}: \mbox{`Type of twin` and `whether convicted` are independent}. $$
It seems the alternative one would set out to prove is
one-sided, reflecting a higher conviction rate among
monozygotic twins.  In that regard, our $P$-value should
reflect results as extreme or more so than 10 in the
bottom left cell.  That is the value produced by the
command
```{r}
1-phyper(9, 13, 17, 12)
```

We might simulate this probability using **permutation
testing**.  We maintain the marginal totals, but shuffle
one variable.  To do so, changes the counts in the table
itself.  Here is one run.
```{r}
tally(type ~ shuffle(record), data=twins)
```

When we repeat this many times, we will grab just the
value in the 2nd row, 1st column.
```{r}
simCornerValue <- replicate(50000,
          tally(type ~ shuffle(record), data=twins)[2,1]
          )
head(simCornerValue)
```

We find the proportion of values higher than 10:
```{r}
prop(~(simCornerValue >= 10))
```
This is reasonably close to the value $0.0004652$
found earlier using `phyper()`.
